title: GPU Eval Quarantine and CI Throttling Policy
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary:

This document defines the policy and operational playbook for quarantining high-impact evaluation (eval) workloads and applying CI-side throttles to protect production and shared GPU fleet capacity. It covers build-time controls, CI pipeline rate limits, tenant quarantine criteria, automated enforcement via IaC/CI tooling, and remediation/runbook steps for oncall engineers.

Purpose and scope:

- Purpose: Prevent eval/e2e/benchmark pipelines from causing production degradation, cross-tenant interference, and unexpected billing spikes while preserving fast developer iteration for low-risk workloads.
- Scope: All GPU-backed CI jobs, ephemeral eval clusters, and scheduled benchmark pipelines that consume shared inferencing or training GPU pools across public cloud accounts managed by Redwood Inference. Does not apply to isolated Dedicated capacity (customers with reserved physical pools) unless configured by their account owner.

Definitions:

- Eval workload: CI job that runs model evals, end-to-end benchmarks, or long-running metric collection tasks that use GPU resources for > 10 minutes.
- Quarantine: Automatic isolation of a tenant's eval jobs into a limited-capacity sandbox pool and enforcement of stricter rate limits until a manual review or time-based release.
- Tokenized quota: A lightweight credit token assigned to CI pipelines representing allowed GPU-minutes per day/week for eval workloads.

Policy principles:

1) Lowest privilege by default: New eval pipelines start with a conservative token allotment and may request increases through a self-serve flow.
2) Protect production-first: Production-facing jobs and preflight release tests are prioritized over eval or non-blocking e2e runs.
3) Automated detection + manual review: Quarantines are primarily automated based on thresholds; all quarantines generate an alert and a short review window.
4) Transparent economics: Token consumption and billing attribution must be visible in the Redwood Console and CI logs.

Thresholds and triggers (config table):

- Threshold name | Trigger condition | Immediate action
- ----------------------------------------------
- Burst spike | Tenant uses > 300 GPU-minutes in any rolling 60m window | Immediate throttle to 20% of prior concurrency & enqueue quarantine review
- Prolonged high load | Tenant uses > 1200 GPU-minutes/day | Quarantine tenant to sandbox pool, reduce concurrency to 1 job, notify team
- Preempt rate | > 10% spot preemptions for tenant over 6 hours | Move eval jobs to preempt-tolerant sandbox; reduce burst allowance
- Failed cleanup | > 5 orphaned GPU attachments in 24h from tenant | Block new ephemeral allocations until cleanup performed

Implementation details (how enforcement works):

- Token system: Implemented as a lightweight service (eval-quota-svc) backed by Redis and integrated into CI runner hooks. Each pipeline requests tokens before scheduling GPU pods. Tokens are deducted per GPU-minute and can be donated between teams via a simple API.
- CI runner hooks: GitLab/GitHub Actions runner wrapper makes a pre-flight token request; if denied, job exits with code 79 and logs reason. Runners also support backoff and queueing with ETA annotation for builds in the Console.
- Terraform/IaC: Quarantine and sandbox pool resources are defined in terraform modules under modules/ci-eval-sandbox. The module creates a restricted nodepool label (kube taint: eval-quarantine=true, tolerations required) and network egress policies to limit downstream bandwidth and endpoint access.

Example IaC snippet (usage):

terraform module "ci_eval_sandbox" {
  source = "git::ssh://git.internal/redwood/modules//ci-eval-sandbox"
  cluster = var.cluster_id
  max_gpu_nodes = 4
  node_labels = { "purpose" = "eval-quarantine" }
}

CI pipeline integration examples:

- Pre-flight step (bash):
  - ./ci-tools/request-eval-tokens --tenant $TENANT --gpu-minutes $ESTIMATED_MINUTES || exit 79
- Post-job step:
  - ./ci-tools/return-eval-tokens --job-id $CI_JOB_ID --unused-minutes $UNUSED

Observability and metrics to monitor:

- Dashboard metrics (Console):
  - eval_quota_consumption: per-tenant GPU-minutes/day
  - eval_quota_rate: token grant/deny rate
  - sandbox_pool_utilization: node/gpu utilization %
  - preempt_rate_by_tenant: spot preemptions 1h/6h
  - orphaned_gpu_attachments: count by tenant

- Alerts and SLOs:
  - P1: Quarantine triggered for > 5 tenants in 15 minutes -> Pager to infra-oncall (SLO: 99.9% availability of eviction-safe enforcement)
  - P2: Token service error rate > 1% 10m -> Paging to infra-backend oncall
  - Reporting: Weekly quota usage report emailed to infra-owners and team leads

Runbook: Quarantine event (step-by-step)

1) Detection: Alert fires (quarantine-created) in PagerDuty; ticket auto-created in JIRA with tag ci-quarantine-automated.
2) Initial triage (5-15m):
  - Oncall reads alert runbook and dashboard.
  - Verify tenant ID, job IDs, and offending pipelines in Console.
  - Check token service logs: grant/deny history for tenant.
3) Immediate mitigation (15-30m):
  - If production impact observed (increased latency, error budget burn), escalate to infra-sre channel and follow the production failover playbook.
  - If no production impact, keep quarantine but contact tenant owners via automated email + slack with remediation checklist.
4) Remediation checklist for tenant owners:
  - Inspect pipeline to identify runaway loops or forgotten infinite loops.
  - Reduce concurrency flags and add pre-flight token checks to all jobs.
  - Compact or shard eval workloads across time windows using cron windows.
  - Request temporary token increase using self-serve form with justification and budget owner sign-off.
5) Release (post-review):
  - After tenant remediation verified by infra (verify token consumption drop for 24h), remove quarantine via terraform apply on the module to remove taint and increase allowed concurrency.
  - Update Jira with root-cause and closure notes.

Escalation matrix:

- Tier 1 (infra-oncall): initial triage and token service flakiness (15m).
- Tier 2 (platform-engineering): sandbox pool sizing, IaC errors, network egress constraints (30-60m).
- Tier 3 (infra-leads): policy exceptions, billing disputes, and cross-account network issues (2-6h).

Self-serve policy and exception flow:

- Small increases (< 25% extra daily quota) can be requested via the Console UI; auto-approved if team has < 2 prior quarantines in 30 days.
- Medium/large increases require a short form and approval by platform-eng and finance-owner. Approval results in temporary token grants tied to a billing code.
- Emergency exceptions: platform leads can issue ephemeral tokens (time-limited) for urgent investigative runs. All emergency grants are logged and require post-hoc review.

Network and security constraints for sandbox pools:

- Egress fencing: Sandbox nodes use a dedicated NAT gateway with rate-limited egress and a WAF rule set to block known high-cost endpoints (e.g., public model hosting buckets not whitelisted).
- KMS/HSM: No customer secrets are accessible from sandbox pools by default; if a pipeline needs temporary access, use a scoped short-lived role which must be approved via the exception flow.

CI/CD and Release gating implications:

- Release pipelines that are marked production-critical are exempt from eval throttles but must be registered with release-policy CI tags and run in isolated nodepools.
- Non-blocking regression suites should be labeled with ci:low-priority to be queued behind production and quarantined evals when capacity contention occurs.

Post-incident analysis and feedback loop:

- After each quarantine event, platform-eng will run a 15-minute postmortem within 48 hours capturing: root cause, remediation steps taken, IaC changes applied, and lessons learned.
- Quarterly: Review token allotments and sandbox sizing based on aggregate quota utilization and billing data.

Operational runbook snippets (commands):

- View sandbox pool usage:
  - kubectl --context $SANDBOX get nodes -l purpose=eval-quarantine -o wide
- Force release a tenant from quarantine (admin-only):
  - terraform workspace select infra-prod && terraform apply -target=module.ci_eval_sandbox.module.quarantine_release -var tenant_id=$TENANT_ID
- Revoke orphaned GPU attachments:
  - ./infra-tools/cleanup-orphaned-gpus --tenant $TENANT_ID --dry-run

Ownership and responsibilities:

- Platform Engineering: maintain eval-quota-svc, Terraform modules, and console integration.
- Infra SRE: oncall for enforcement alerts, runbook execution, and production impact escalation.
- Developer Platform (DX): owner of CI runner wrappers and self-serve token request flows.
- Finance & Billing: periodic audit of token grants tied to billing codes.

C. FAQ:

Q: What if my eval runs are legitimately large?
A: Use the self-serve increase flow with a short justification and attach a billing code; for sustained high usage consider moving to Dedicated capacity.

Q: How long does quarantine last?
A: Standard quarantine is 24–72 hours pending remediation; extensions require documented review.
